title: Roo and the Whoosh Ghost
markdown:
The meadow woke before Roo did. Sunshine found the daisies first, then the burrow mouth, then the long legs of a kangaroo joey still half in a stretch. Roo bounced out anyway. His hops were the bounciest in the grass, and his ears wiggled as if they had their own morning to finish. Butterflies lifted off the clover. Bees kept their busy thread of sound. The whole meadow felt like a playground that had been waiting for him.

His best friend was Gossamer, a curtain fairy no bigger than a pocket handkerchief. She lived in a soft sunny window curtain at the edge of the field, where the cloth smelled of warm cotton and sweet clover. Her wings were lace that had learned to fly. When she laughed, it sounded like tiny bells testing themselves. Every day she fluttered from the curtain, ready for whatever the daisies were doing.

The daisies loved the sun. Their yellow faces nodded in the breeze, and Roo and Gossamer liked to lean close and whisper secrets into the petals, as if flowers could keep a confidence better than pockets.

Then someone new came. A shy ghost named Whisper, so quiet his feet made no sound at all. He floated through the meadow wanting a friend. He watched the daisies dance. But when he passed, a soft airy whoosh lifted their heads and set them down again all wrong. Yellow faces drooped. Petals folded in a little, surprised, as if a tiny sigh had gone through the flowers without asking.

Roo saw the droop and tilted his head. His nose twitched.

“The daisies look a bit sad. Their heads are all down.”

Gossamer flew closer. She saw the tucked petals.

“It is not the sunshine. It is the whoosh. Too much of a surprise.”

They watched Whisper float by again. More daisies folded. Roo felt a flutter in his tummy, the kind that comes when something new arrives and the grass does not know what to do with it. Whisper did not look like trouble. He looked like a cloud that had forgotten how to sit in the sky.

“We should help him,” Roo said, and thumped his tail once, not as a speech, only as a decision.

“He does not mean to surprise them,” Gossamer said. “He just floats.”

They hopped and fluttered to the edge of the meadow, where the oak trees made cool shadows. Whisper sat on a mossy stone, watching the happy daisies he could not join. He looked a little sad, like weather without sun.

“Hello, Whisper,” Roo called, warm enough not to startle a ghost if a ghost could be startled.

Whisper jumped a little. The jump made an airy sound, almost nothing.

“Oh. Hello, Roo. Hello, Gossamer.”

Gossamer landed on a dewy blade of grass.

“We saw the daisies. They droop when you float by.”

Whisper sighed. It sounded like wind in dry leaves.

“I do not mean to. My feet just whoosh. I want to be friends. I do not want to scare them.” He looked at his see-through feet, which looked as if they were already halfway gone.

“We can help,” Roo said, bouncing once and then holding still so the moss would not think he was leaving. “Gossamer knows about soft breezes.”

Gossamer’s voice came out like the lightest air.

“If you think about floating as slowly as a falling leaf, your feet can be even quieter. You can be like a secret guest.”

Roo nudged Whisper, gentle as a dandelion against a knee.

“Or think of a dandelion puff. Those little white seeds that go away on the air and never stamp.”

Whisper’s ghostly eyes widened.

“A dandelion puff?”

“Yes,” Roo said. “Imagine you are as light as a seed. Think light. Think soft. Think slow.”

Whisper closed his eyes. He took a quiet breath. He imagined a warm breeze and a fluffy seed so light it danced without a sound. He imagined himself that light. When he opened his eyes and drifted, the daisies’ petals only trembled, like tiny sunbeams deciding to stay. The meadow kept its bee-hum. The air felt soft as a feather and smelled of warm grass.

“Thank you,” Whisper whispered. “That was better. I can float and be friends.”

After that he moved through the meadow with a soft flutter. The daisies kept their faces up. Roo did not say helping was the best play. He only bounced once beside the mossy stone, Gossamer ringing a small laugh into the sun, and Whisper practiced being a seed until even the nearest daisy forgot to fold.
